newsitem.title: NETHERLANDS: U.S. may block Croatia control over E.Slavonia.
newsitem.headline: U.S. may block Croatia control over E.Slavonia.

text.p: The United States may back a delay in Croatia resuming control of the U.N.-administered enclave of Eastern Slavonia if Zagreb does not permit exiled ethnic Serbs to return to their homes there, the State Department said on Wednesday.

"It's entirely possible that the United States will have to vote to extend the mandate of the U.N. military mission in Eastern Slavonia is there isn't better Croatian performance" on the refugee issue, spokesman Nicholas Burns told reporters.

The United States and its European allies involved in bringing peace to the Balkans have been angered by Croatia's stubborn refusal to permit 350,000 exiled ethnic Serbs to return to their pre-war homes.
The region was seized six years ago by rebel Serbs but plans for its return to Croatian control were laid under terms of the 1995 Dayton peace agreement which ended the war in ex-Yugoslavia.
U.S.Secretary of State Madeleine Albright is expected to discuss this issue, among others, when she meets Croatian President Franjo Tudjman in Zagreb on Saturday.
She also plans to meet Serbian President Slobodan Milosevic in Belgrade the same day and hold talks with Bosnian President Alija Izetbegovic in Sarajevo on Sunday.
She is pressing a U.S. campaign to re-invigorate the Dayton accord and make sure that all aspects of the U.S.-brokered peace agreement are implemented.
If the U.N. Security Council votes in June, as some predict, to extend the U.N. mandate in Eastern Slavonia, it would add to frictions in ties between Washington and Zagreb.

Croatian Foreign Minister Mate Granic and his delegation were said by U.S. officials to have been shaken by a recent meeting in Washington in which Albright reportedly delivered a tough message on U.S. plans to deny Zagreb access to international lending, membership in NATO's Partnership for Peace organisation and other western institutions if it does not comply fully with the peace agreement.
